Mountain Climbing. The sport and practice of ascending mountains for sport, exploration, or conquest, evolving from extreme mountaineers testing themselves against Alpine peaks into a global pursuit encompassing diverse techniques and environments.

Modern mountaineering emerged in the Alps during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Climbers like Horace-Bénédict de Saussure pioneered Alpine ascents for scientific and sporting purposes.

The Matterhorn, a spectacular four thousand four hundred seventy-eight meter peak in the Alps, became an iconic symbol of mountaineering when first successfully climbed in eighteen sixty-five. The ascent sparked the modern mountaineering movement.

Mount Everest, the world's highest mountain at eight thousand eight hundred forty-nine meters, was first summited in nineteen fifty-three by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay. Reaching Everest has become a goal for wealthy climbers worldwide.

K two, the world's second-highest mountain, remains far more dangerous than Everest. Approximately one in four climbers attempting K two die, making it the mountaineer's ultimate test.

The Seven Summits challenge—climbing the highest peak on each continent—has become a major goal in modern mountaineering since the nineteen eighties, popularized by mountaineer Dick Bass.

Modern mountaineering employs sophisticated equipment including ropes, pitons, carabiners, oxygen systems, and protective gear. Altitude sickness and avalanches remain the greatest dangers.

Women have progressively broken mountaineering's gender barriers. Junko Tabei was the first woman to summit Everest in nineteen seventy-five, opening the sport to broader participation.

High-altitude mountaineering faces extreme environmental hazards. The death zone above eight thousand meters has insufficient oxygen for human acclimatization, and climbers risk pulmonary edema and cerebral edema.

The commercialization of Everest climbing has created ethical tensions between accessibility, environmental preservation, and the physical and psychological demands of mountaineering.
